plan.contextChunk: This figure presents three side-by-side ray diagrams, labeled (a), (b), and (c), each showing light meeting a flat horizontal boundary between two media. In every panel a shaded blue rectangle fills the lower half and carries the label n1 at its right edge, the unshaded region above it is labeled n2, and a vertical dashed line marks the normal at the point of incidence. In panel (a) a solid ray annotated Incident ray travels up and to the right inside n1 and splits at the surface: a Refracted ray continues into n2, tilted away from the normal at the marked angle theta_2, while a Reflected ray turns back down into n1 at theta_1, matching the incident angle theta_1 marked on the other side of the normal. Panel (b) shows a steeper incident ray drawn at the angle labeled theta_c, whose refracted ray now runs flat along the interface with a small square and the label theta_2 = 90 degrees, and whose reflected ray leaves at theta_c. In panel (c) the incident ray arrives at theta_1, larger than the dashed reference ray drawn at theta_c beside it, and no refracted ray appears at all, only a reflected ray next to the words Total internal reflection. Read left to right the three panels track one incident angle being steadily increased, which defines the critical angle and the condition under which light is confined entirely to the medium of higher index.

interactions.label: Incident angle theta1
interactions.teaches: The three panels are not separate phenomena but consecutive regimes reached as theta1 increases: below the critical angle light refracts, at the critical angle the refracted ray lies along the boundary, and above it there is total internal reflection

demo_steps.title: Ordinary refraction
demo_steps.narration: Panel (a) stays visible in the triptych while it is highlighted: the incident ray partly reflects and partly refracts into n2, bending away from the normal.

demo_steps.title: Critical angle
demo_steps.narration: Panel (b) is highlighted at the threshold case. The refracted ray lies exactly along the boundary, so the diagram must show theta2 = 90 degrees and the right-angle marker.

demo_steps.title: Total internal reflection

interactionPlan.keyInsight: The critical angle is the transition point where the refracted ray reaches 90 degrees; beyond that, refraction cannot occur and the ray is totally internally reflected.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Preserve the original three-panel triptych as the default view: panels (a), (b), and (c) should always remain side by side, with interactivity only adding a subtle highlight or faint overlay, never replacing the triptych with one enlarged single diagram. Do not show a dashed theta_c reference, theta_c label, formula line, or status banner in the ordinary refraction panel. If any angle-sweep overlay is drawn, keep it visually separate from the source-style panel labels and make it faint enough not to read as part of the original panel. Use a light-blue lower medium and white upper medium in all three panels, separated by a horizontal boundary with a dashed vertical normal. Ray geometry should progress from refracted upward ray in panel (a), to boundary-parallel refracted ray with theta2 = 90 degrees and a right-angle marker in panel (b), to no transmitted ray and a clear 'Total internal reflection' label in panel (c). Recreate the textbook-style black curved or wavy callout arrows for the Incident ray, Reflected ray, and Refracted ray labels rather than using straight leader lines. Panel (c) should include the source-style dashed reference ray layout, but it must not be confused with an actual refracted ray.

authoredContext:
Consider what happens when a ray of light strikes the surface between two materials, as shown in the figure(a). Part of the light crosses the boundary and is refracted; the rest is reflected. If, as shown in the figure, the index of refraction for the second medium is less than for the first, the ray bends away from the perpendicular. (Since n1>n2, the angle of refraction is greater than the angle of incidence—that is, θ2>θ1.) Now imagine what happens as the incident angle increases. This causes θ2 to increase also. The largest the angle of refraction θ2 can be is 90°, as shown in part (b). The critical angle θc for a combination of materials is defined to be the incident angle θ1 that produces an angle of refraction of 90°. That is, θc is the incident angle for which θ2=90°. If the incident angle θ1 is greater than the critical angle, as shown in the figure(c), then all of the light is reflected back into medium 1, a condition called total internal reflection. (As the figure shows, the reflected rays obey the law of reflection so that the angle of reflection is equal to the angle of incidence in all three cases.)

Total internal reflection occurs for any incident angle greater than the critical angle θc, and it can only occur when the second medium has an index of refraction less than the first. Note that this equation is written for a light ray that travels in medium 1 and reflects from medium 2, as shown in the figure.

(a) A ray of light crosses a boundary where the index of refraction decreases. That is, n2<n1. The ray bends away from the perpendicular. (b) The critical angle θc is the angle of incidence for which the angle of refraction is 90°. (c) Total internal reflection occurs when the incident angle is greater than the critical angle.

In figure a, an incident ray at an angle theta 1 with a perpendicular line drawn at the point of incidence travels from n 1 to n 2. The incident ray undergoes both refraction and reflection. The angle of refraction o the refracted ray in medium n 2 is theta 2. The angle of reflection of the reflected ray in medium 1 is theta 1. In figure b, the incident angle is theta c which is larger than the angle of incidence in figure a. The angle of refraction theta 2 becomes 90 degrees and the angle of reflection is theta c. In figure c, the angle of incidence theta 1 is greater than theta c, total internal reflection takes place and only reflection takes place. The light ray travels back into medium n 1, with the reflection angle being theta one.

interactions.label: Incident angle theta1
interactions.teaches: As theta1 increases, the refracted ray bends farther away from the normal until it reaches 90 degrees at theta_c; beyond that point, no transmitted ray exists and all light is reflected internally

interactions.label: Index ratio n2/n1
interactions.teaches: Changing n2/n1 moves the critical-angle reference because theta_c is determined by sin(theta_c) = n2/n1; smaller ratios make total internal reflection begin at smaller incident angles

demo_steps.title: Ordinary refraction
demo_steps.narration: With theta1 below theta_c, part of the light reflects back into n1 and part refracts into n2. Because n1 is greater than n2, the refracted ray bends away from the normal.

demo_steps.title: The critical angle
demo_steps.narration: Increase theta1 until it reaches theta_c. The refracted ray now lies exactly along the boundary, so theta2 equals 90 degrees.

demo_steps.title: Total internal reflection
demo_steps.narration: Past theta_c, the refracted ray disappears. The light remains entirely in the original medium as a reflected ray.

demo_steps.title: Changing the index ratio
demo_steps.narration: Lower n2/n1 and watch the dashed theta_c reference move closer to the normal. The same incident angle can switch from transmitting to totally internally reflecting because the critical angle has changed.

plan.keyInsight: Total internal reflection begins exactly when the refracted ray would need to bend past 90 degrees, which is impossible, so the critical angle is the boundary between transmission and confinement.
plan.reconstructionNotes: Use a single enlarged ray diagram rather than three fixed panels, but preserve the visual language of the original figure: blue lower rectangle for n1, white upper region for n2, a horizontal interface, and a dashed vertical normal. Draw rays in teal with arrowheads. The incident and reflected rays should always be visible and symmetric about the normal. The refracted ray should rotate away from the normal as theta1 increases, become horizontal at theta_c, and fade out or vanish for total internal reflection. Show a dashed critical-angle reference ray in the lower medium, with theta_c labeled, so learners can compare the current theta1 against the threshold. Include small state references labeled (a), (b), and (c) or a compact status caption to connect the dynamic view to the original three-panel progression.

interactions.teaches: The three panels are not separate phenomena but consecutive regimes reached as theta1 increases: below the critical angle light refracts, at the critical angle the refracted ray lies along the boundary, and above it there is total internal reflection

demo_steps.title: Ordinary refraction
demo_steps.narration: Panel (a) stays visible in the triptych while it is highlighted: the incident ray partly reflects and partly refracts into n2, bending away from the normal.

demo_steps.title: Critical angle
demo_steps.narration: Panel (b) is highlighted at the threshold case. The refracted ray lies exactly along the boundary, so the diagram must show theta2 = 90 degrees and the right-angle marker.

demo_steps.title: Total internal reflection
demo_steps.narration: Panel (c) is highlighted after theta1 exceeds the critical angle. The refracted ray is absent, and the light remains in n1 as a reflected ray.

plan.keyInsight: The critical angle is the transition point where the refracted ray reaches 90 degrees; beyond that, refraction cannot occur and the ray is totally internally reflected.

Use a light-blue lower medium and white upper medium in all three panels, separated by a horizontal boundary with a dashed vertical normal. Ray geometry should progress from refracted upward ray in panel (a), to boundary-parallel refracted ray with theta2 = 90 degrees and a right-angle marker in panel (b), to no transmitted ray and a clear 'Total internal reflection' label in panel (c). Recreate the textbook-style black curved or wavy callout arrows for the Incident ray, Reflected ray, and Refracted ray labels rather than using straight leader lines. Panel (c) should include the source-style dashed reference ray layout, but it must not be confused with an actual refracted ray.
